title: Rosalind and the Hymn
premise: Kestrel Nystrom, a tunnel-mapping urban explorer who survives by counting doors and keeping lights on, returns home to find Rosalind — the imaginary friend they buried at age nine — waiting on the porch, unchanged. Rosalind leads them into unmapped tunnels beneath the town where their missing mother once sang a hymn that binds a hungry, patient thing; every verse sung aloud feeds it, and the last verse was never written down. To end it, Kestrel must recover the final verse from the memories of the dead who learned it, without ever singing along themselves. In the flooded dark, Kestrel sings it silently, gives Rosalind the goodbye they never got as a child, and walks out alone into morning — carrying the song's memory but never its voice.
about_author: Quentin Voss is the pen name of a former municipal surveyor who spent a decade documenting infrastructure that official maps insisted did not exist. They write horror about places that remember people better than people remember themselves.

chapters.title: The Porch Light Rule
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Returning from a mapping job, Kestrel finds Rosalind on the porch — exactly as they left her twenty years ago, down to the crooked smile. The emotional beat is dread braided with longing: the found-family wound reopening. Kestrel lets her in against every rule they've built to stay safe.

chapters.title: Doors That Count Themselves
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Rosalind doesn't eat, sleep, or age, and the apartment's doors begin recounting overnight — one extra each dawn. Kestrel investigates her origin in childhood records and finds their mother's hymnal, pages torn out. The beat is mounting unease: comfort curdling into evidence that something followed them home.

chapters.title: Below the Survey Line
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Rosalind asks to be taken to the tunnels; Kestrel agrees, telling themselves it's reconnaissance. Beneath town they find corridors no survey shows, walls scored with tally marks matching Kestrel's own door-counting habit. The beat is vertigo — the explorer realizing the map has been exploring them.

chapters.title: The Congregation of Echoes
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, first time. She remembers being imagined: born from a lonely child's need, then abandoned mid-song when Kestrel's mother vanished. She reveals the hymn is a lullaby for something older than the town, and the last verse keeps it asleep. Her beat is grief — love that became a leash.

chapters.title: What Mother Left Unsung
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. In the flooded lower gallery, Kestrel finds their mother's camp: decades old, still warm. A recording plays half the hymn before the tape chews itself. Kestrel hums along involuntarily and the tunnel answers. The beat is terror and inheritance — realizing they were always meant to finish this.

chapters.title: Verse by Verse
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Rosalind teaches Kestrel the first verses so they can navigate safely, warning: hear it, hold it, never voice it. Each verse Kestrel memorizes, a memory of their childhood goes missing instead. The beat is bargain-making dread — trading the past for passage through it.

chapters.title: The Neighbors Below
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Other explorers who mapped these tunnels are found standing in the dark, singing in unison, faces serene. Among them, someone wearing Kestrel's mother's coat turns and greets them by name. The beat is horror of recognition — the congregation wants a family reunion, and Kestrel is the guest of honor.

chapters.title: Rosalind's Confession
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She admits she led Kestrel here deliberately: the thing below promised to make her real if she delivered the child who stopped singing. But watching Kestrel lose memories, she chooses Kestrel over existence. The beat is devastating tenderness — the imaginary friend becoming the realest person in the story.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, climax. At the hymn's source — a chamber like a throat — the congregation closes in, singing the eighth verse, demanding the ninth from Kestrel's mouth. Kestrel reconstructs the final verse from their stolen memories, sings it silently, breath shaping words without sound. The thing starves mid-reach; the tunnels begin collapsing. The beat is white-knuckle triumph bought with everything.

chapters.title: Counting Doors in Daylight
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, resolution. Kestrel surfaces at dawn, memories partially returned, Rosalind gone — dissolved mid-goodbye, finally finished rather than abandoned. Weeks later, Kestrel seals the survey gap officially and leaves the porch light on anyway, a habit kept for a friend only they remember. The beat is bittersweet peace: found family doesn't have to survive to count.
